quotes.text: Yeah, so Blind Tiger came to me with a really interesting problem to solve — they had this old wallpaper that covered the vestibule area, around the stairs, and up to the second floor and they were like, "hey, we want to do something with this. Do you think you could paint on top of this?" I've never painted on top of wallpaper before, but I love this kind of challenge so I got a sample of the wallpaper and tested out different kinds of paints — it was definitely a first all the way around.

There's often statements and lettering within my work but with this one I didn't want to do that, I wanted to just do larger shapes. And I wanted some of the wallpaper to still be seen, so I used a light wash. I basically had a chemistry set — I had thinner, and I had water and I tested out different mixtures to see which one would get us to the point where the paint would be transparent but not run down the wall.

One of the shapes that I used was just the open wallpaper, so when you see it there's a couple different tones of browns and grays and then there's some open spaces, that's the original wallpaper. And since I did a wash on the other shapes you can kind of see the pattern in the wallpaper and it really pops.

It was a really unique project. I had a blast with it, and it's still one of my favorites I've done yet. The freedom they allowed on this project just allowed for me to nerd out. That's kind of how it all started.

No, this was a solo one. Rachel's got this mastery of color, just on another level, so I'll often come up with a color palette and be like, "hey, does this work?" But for the Carleton mural I did the colors on my own.

Language plays a huge role in my work. A lot of my work is based around letter forms and has statements involved, so the idea of being able to communicate very complex emotions in the shortest and quickest way has always really fascinated me.

I love listening to poets and musicians because they're able to encapsulate this human experience into like four or five lines. That's always really impressed me and it's something I've wanted to do through my work. I keep notes to myself about certain experiences and things I need to either work through or that I want to express in the work, and try to figure out how to say it in the least amount of space and convey exactly how I'm feeling.
It's a mix of both. Sometimes there'll be a song lyric or a line from a poem that really hits and I'm like, oh, I couldn't say that any better.

Yeah, even when I do get inspiration from someone else I try to distill it down from there. Most of the time I have running notes of things that pop into my head. That's what I was doing while spacing out on a ladder yesterday; I just needed like two more words; so I kind of jostle with that, trying to slim things down. It's so difficult to keep it short, but it's also a fun part of the challenge and expression for me.
I imagined Ryan working in a similar way, writing on average, one or two songs per day.
Ryan seemed to think that it was not his decision to make. You, dear reader, should be the one to judge if a song has merit or not.
I haven't had the problem yet of having a number one record, and then having to figure out what do I do to try to ruin this moment so I could go back to making other stuff.
